claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC state.
Slow cooling and annealing enable differential substitutional-element mobility, particularly involving Ni and Al.
Differential atomic mobility produces nanoscale Ni- and Al-enriched or depleted regions in the BCC matrix.
Annealing of a BCC multi-principal-element alloy can be accompanied by phase decomposition and an inhomogeneous elemental distribution.
The proposed compositional gradients are nanoscale.
Local compositional gradients reduce the thermodynamic nucleation barrier.
The compositionally modulated regions act as heterogeneous nucleation sites.
Barrier reduction at compositionally modulated regions initiates secondary-phase formation.
The secondary phases formed in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 may include FCC or intermetallic phases.
Thermal-history differences can alter phase fractions and nucleation behavior in multicomponent alloys.
Rapid quenching suppresses atomic diffusion and elemental partitioning.
Rapidly quenched Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 remains a homogeneous, single-phase metastable BCC material.
Slow cooling at approximately 1–10 K/min followed by holds at 600–800 °C provides enough mobility for measurable partitioning.
Slow-cooled and annealed samples will show compositional fluctuations spatially correlated with secondary phases.
Slow-cooled and annealed samples will have a greater secondary-phase fraction than rapidly quenched samples.
The hypothesis should apply at 600–800 °C under slow cooling but not when cooling is fast enough to make diffusion negligible.
The controlled test compares identically prepared, rapidly quenched samples against samples slowly cooled at 1–10 K/min and annealed at 600–800 °C.

Failure to detect statistically significant compositional gradients or an increased secondary-phase fraction in the slow-cooled and annealed group, with both groups remaining similarly uniform BCC, would falsify the hypothesis.
